newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal edges closer to meeting EMU test.
newsitem.headline: Portugal edges closer to meeting EMU test.

text.p: Portugal edged closer to membership of a European single currency on Wednesday when the European Union's statistics body Eurostat showed it was making progress on one of the key economic tests for entry.
The Finance Ministry said that a new definition drawn up by Eurostat would allow it to lop nearly five percentage points off the ratio between the country's debt and gross domestic product (GDP).
Under the new rules it forecast the ratio would be 64.3 percent in 1997, the year on which aspiring member nations of economic and monetary union (EMU) will be judged.

That takes Portugal down from the 69 percent initially forecast. In theory, candidate countries should have a debt-to-GDP ratio of just 60 percent but the EU's Maastricht Treaty blueprint gives almost equal importance to the fact that a ratio is falling.
Some countries whose membership of EMU is usually taken for granted, Belgium for example, have debt-to-GDP ratios significantly above the ceiling.

Analysts said that the closer countries such as Portugal, once seen as only an outside bet for EMU, got to meeting fully all the entry tests, the more difficult it would be for their European partners to keep them out of a single currency due to be launched in 1999.
The EU's 15 member states will decide in spring 1998 which countries have qualified based on economic performance this year.
"(This revision) puts Portugal closer to monetary union, more for political reasons than anything else," said analyst Isabel Cabral of Lisbon brokers Fincor.
The Finance Ministry said the revision of the debt figures, brought about by accounting changes to the way some interest rates are booked, would not affect its budget deficit forecasts.
The government has budgeted for a deficit of 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997, inside the EMU limit of three percent and down from four percent last year.
With inflation under tight rein, government officials had said that the debt ratio was about the only EMU criterion that Portugal could not satisfy.
"The important thing was to show that the (debt) trend was declining...but this puts us in a stronger position, politically," said Carlos Pinto Ferreira, an analyst with Banco Cisf.
"It puts us in a better position than Spain," he added. Spain's debt-to-GDP ratio was some 69 percent in 1996 against 66 percent the year before.
